newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi says U.N. floats request for Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: Burundi says U.N. floats request for Zaire force.

text.p: The U.N. special envoy for the Zaire crisis has sounded out Burundi's isolated military government about logistics help for a planned multinational force, a senior Burundian official said on Sunday.
Raymond Chretien raised the idea on Friday during talks in Bujumbura with President Pierre Buyoya, he said.

"We have received an exploratory request about using Bujumbura airport and port to help the effort for refugees in eastern Zaire," Buyoya's spokesman, Jean-Luc Ndizeye, told Reuters in Nairobi by telephone.
"The idea was raised by Mr Chretien on Friday. President Buyoya said he was willing to discuss it but that in principle Burundi was ready to help as much as possible," Ndizeye said.
Chretien, currently in Rwanda, was not immediately available for comment.
Landlocked Burundi, bordered by Rwanda to the north and rebel-held eastern Zaire to the west, is diplomatically and economically isolated.
Regional states imposed a total trade embargo on July 31, in protest against Buyoya's coup six days earlier.

Burundi stands to gain politically if the U.N.-backed force, which is yet to be deployed, uses Bujumbura to ferry aid to hundreds of thousands of distressed Hutu refugees believed to be across the border in east Zaire's South Kivu province.
There were 230,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees around the town of Uvira in South Kivu before Zairean rebels captured the area last month, causing the refugees to flee.
"De facto the force would break the embargo and secure Buyoya's position politically and diplomatically," one regional analyst, who declined to be quoted by name, told Reuters.

The regional states who imposed the embargo, led by Tanzania and Kenya, will expect to be consulted before the U.N. takes a decision and are unlikely to favour any move which would weaken the pressure on Major Buyoya and his minority Tutsi army.
They want him to enter power-sharing talks with exiled leaders of the Hutu majority.

But the options are limited for the Canadian-led force if it wants to reach the Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees in South Kivu. Initial planning was to help them from the border town of Bukavu, north of Uvira.
But the main volunteer for that task, France, is opposed by both the Zairean rebels in control of Bukavu and Rwanda across the border.

France has reasonable relations with Buyoya's Burundi and if he provided adequate security assurance the Bujumbura option would allow French troops to get involved in the international relief effort, analysts noted.
Buyoya's hand has strengthened by the day because Hutu rebel bases in eastern Zaire have been closed by the ethnic Tutsi Zairean rebels now in control there.
Buyoya said on Sunday Hutu activity had now switched to Tanzania, home to 660,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees.

"The fact is that the rebellion is clearly moving from Zaire to Tanzania - this is certain, these are observable facts," Buyoya told Radio France Internationale after meeting former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere on Saturday.
"He (Nyerere) himself does not deny it, since the staff of the rebellion can be found today to be settled in Tanzania," Buyoya said.
Nyerere is international mediator for the conflict in Burundi, overshadowed by events in Zaire but previously Africa's bloodiest ethnic civil war.
